name: Cryolipolysis (CoolSculpting Mini Chin)

lead: Cryolipolysis uses controlled cold to reduce small pockets of fat. Under the chin it is one of the sites cleared by the US FDA, and a smaller applicator is sometimes marketed as a mini-chin treatment, giving a leaner jawline and neck without surgery.

Cold is intended to damage fat tissue in the treated area, which the body then gradually clears over following months. Systematic reviews report average fat-thickness reductions of a few millimeters and high patient satisfaction, and reviewers describe the data quality as low.

paras: A device cools the skin and fat in the submental area over a set session, with no incision or anesthesia, and people return to normal activity. Results appear gradually over the following months, and people sometimes combine it with weight management.

Commonly reported effects are redness, numbness, swelling, bruising and mild pain, usually resolving within weeks. A rare effect, paradoxical adipose hyperplasia, in which the treated fat enlarges, is reported at roughly 0.12% to 1.0% depending on the study, and surgical options such as liposuction are described for treating it.

angle.text: Users seek fat freezing under the chin for a sharper jawline without surgery. Cold damages fat cells in the area, the body clears them over months, and the jaw-neck line looks leaner. It is FDA-cleared for the area, with modest measured fat reduction in studies.

lead: Cryolipolysis, commonly called fat freezing and sold under the CoolSculpting brand, is a non-invasive procedure that applies controlled cold to the skin to reduce subcutaneous fat in targeted areas.[1] Under the chin it is used to shrink a submental fat pad, the soft fullness often called a double chin, so the jaw-neck line looks sharper and the lower face more defined. The US FDA has cleared the technique for the submental area, along with the jawline, arms, flanks, abdomen and thighs.[1]

In looksmaxxing communities it is discussed as a non-surgical route to a more defined jaw-neck angle, sometimes under the label mini chin, referring to a smaller applicator used for the chin area. People weigh it against alternatives such as deoxycholic acid injections, radiofrequency devices and liposuction; one review of non-surgical neck treatments lists cryolipolysis among the options for submental fat.[2]

Systematic reviews of cryolipolysis across body areas report average fat-thickness reductions and high patient satisfaction, while reviewers rate the quality of the data as low.[1][3] A 2025 meta-analysis of 30 studies found reductions in circumference and fat thickness at 12 weeks, with adverse events commonly reported but mostly mild.[4]

paras: The procedure applies controlled cooling to a fold of skin and fat for a set session. It is performed in a clinic without incisions or anesthesia, and is marketed to people with small, localized fat deposits rather than as a weight-loss method [1].

Zeltiq Aesthetics developed the technology and introduced it in the United States in 2010 under the CoolSculpting name. Allergan Aesthetics acquired Zeltiq in 2017, with the acquisition reported as completed on April 28, 2017 [1].

A 2015 systematic review of 19 studies reported average skinfold-thickness reductions between about 10% and 28.5%, with high satisfaction among patients [1]. A 2023 review of 18 studies reported average ultrasound-measured fat-thickness reductions of 2.0 to 5.1 mm and concluded the procedure appears safe and modestly effective, while rating the quality of the underlying data as low [1].

A 2023 review in the Journal of Cosmetic Dermatology describes the mechanism as cold-induced apoptosis of fat cells, with clearance by macrophages, and reports significant fat-volume reduction and high patient satisfaction while calling for more research in different treatment areas.[5]
Commonly reported effects are redness, numbness, swelling, bruising and mild pain, which usually resolve within weeks [1].

Paradoxical adipose hyperplasia, in which the treated fat grows instead of shrinking, is reported as rare, with published rates ranging from 0.12% to 1.0% depending on the study. Described treatments include liposuction or abdominoplasty [1].

sections.h: Use for the chin and in looksmaxxing communities
paras: A review of non-surgical neck rejuvenation lists percutaneous radiofrequency, radiofrequency-helium plasma, deoxycholic acid injections and cryolipolysis as options for submental preplatysmal fat, and reports percutaneous radiofrequency as having the highest patient satisfaction and lowest complication rate among them.[2] A review of male body contouring notes that men increasingly request body contouring and that cryolipolysis is among the non-invasive devices used, alongside invasive options such as liposuction and jawline fillers.[6]

On looksmax.org, an early thread presented fat freezing as a slower non-invasive form of liposuction and speculated about using it on cheek fat; a user in another thread asked about chin treatment as a man under 30 and noted most online examples are middle-aged women.[7][8] A T Nation member who received two sessions on the love handles reported a visible difference but felt the area returned to its earlier look after a few months.[9]

Reviews of cryolipolysis across body areas are summarized above [1]. A small trial of fat reduction in the submandibular and submental area (14 participants, started February 2016) is registered as completed on ClinicalTrials.gov; no results are given in the registration record available here [10].

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, fat freezing is discussed as a local fat-loss option for the chin and face, with posters asking whether it works for men under 30 and for cheek fat.[7][8]
